title: Hypokalaemia
subject: Medicine
summary: Low serum potassium (<3.5 mmol/L) can cause muscle weakness, arrhythmias and renal loss. Recognise common tropical causes, stage severity, and manage urgently with replacement and cause‑specific therapy.

sections.p: Hypokalaemia is defined as a serum potassium concentration below 3.5 mmol/L. Diagnosis requires a reliable electrolyte measurement, preferably from a venous sample, and exclusion of pseudohypokalaemia (e.g., hemolysis).
b: Serum K⁺ <3.5 mmol/L
Repeat sample if hemolysis suspected
Check accompanying electrolytes (Mg²⁺, Na⁺, Cl⁻)

sections.p: Severity guides urgency of replacement and monitoring.
b: Mild: 3.0–3.4 mmol/L – monitor, oral replacement
Moderate: 2.5–2.9 mmol/L – IV replacement if symptomatic
Severe: <2.5 mmol/L – rapid IV replacement, cardiac monitoring

sections.p: Identify the underlying loss or shift; in low‑resource settings infectious and medication‑related causes are common.
b: Gastro‑intestinal loss – cholera, dysentery, prolonged vomiting
Renal loss – loop/thiazide diuretics, hyperaldosteronism, tubulopathies
Transcellular shift – insulin therapy, β‑agonists, re‑feeding syndrome
Magnesium deficiency – malnutrition, chronic diarrhoea
Herbal remedies & traditional medicines containing laxatives

sections.p: Symptoms reflect muscle and cardiac excitability; severity dictates clinical picture.
b: Mild: fatigue, constipation, mild muscle cramps
Moderate: marked weakness, paresthesiae, palpitations
Severe: flaccid paralysis, ventricular arrhythmias, ECG changes

t.b: Confirms low K⁺; guides severity staging
Detects co‑existing Mg²⁺ deficiency that impairs K⁺ repletion
Distinguishes renal loss (high urine K⁺) from extrarenal loss (low urine K⁺) when urine collection possible
Looks for classic changes (flattened T‑waves, U‑waves, ST depression) that signal cardiac risk

t.a: Stool microscopy / rapid test for cholera or malaria
t.b: Identifies infectious diarrhoea causing K⁺ loss; if unavailable, treat empirically based on clinical picture

b: Severe arrhythmias (ventricular tachycardia, torsades)
Respiratory muscle weakness leading to failure
Progressive paralysis
Concurrent hypomagnesemia worsening refractory hypokalaemia

sections.p: Replace potassium, correct the cause, and monitor.
b: Oral potassium chloride tablets or solution for mild‑moderate cases
IV potassium chloride (10 mmol/L in isotonic saline) for severe or symptomatic cases; give via controlled infusion
Correct magnesium deficiency first if present
Stop or adjust offending diuretics; consider aldosterone antagonists (e.g., spironolactone) if hyperaldosteronism suspected
Treat underlying infection (e.g., rehydration + antibiotics for cholera, antimalarials for malaria)
Avoid rapid IV bolus >20 mmol/L in patients with renal failure or digoxin

sections.p: Ensure stable potassium before discharge and educate on avoidance of precipitating factors.
b: Repeat serum K⁺ and Mg²⁺ 6‑12 h after replacement
Educate on adequate oral rehydration solutions with appropriate K⁺ content
Review diuretic dosing; consider potassium‑sparing agents when chronic diuretic use is needed
Nutritional counselling for malnourished children

sections.p: Conditions that mimic hypokalaemia signs or lab values.
b: Hyperkalaemia – opposite ECG changes (peaked T‑waves)
Hypocalcaemia – also causes tetany but with Chvostek sign
Metabolic alkalosis – can cause intracellular K⁺ shift

sections.p: Laboratory artefacts and co‑existing disorders may mask true potassium status.
b: Hemolysed sample falsely raises K⁺ – repeat test if haemolysis noted
Severe acidosis may shift K⁺ out of cells, giving a normal serum K⁺ despite total body depletion
Low magnesium can cause refractory hypokalaemia; normal K⁺ does not exclude intracellular deficit

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden onset palpitations with ECG changes
Progressive muscle weakness or respiratory difficulty

faq.a: Loss of gastric HCl stimulates renal bicarbonate reabsorption, which promotes renal potassium excretion.

faq.q: Can oral potassium replace severe hypokalaemia?
faq.a: No; severe (<2.5 mmol/L) or symptomatic cases need IV replacement under cardiac monitoring.

faq.q: What ECG change is most specific for hypokalaemia?

exam: A 6‑year‑old with cholera presents with profuse watery stools, vomiting and serum K⁺ 2.8 mmol/L – what is the immediate management and why? — Rapid IV potassium chloride with cardiac monitoring; correct dehydration and replace magnesium first to allow potassium uptake.

A patient on furosemide develops muscle weakness and K⁺ 3.2 mmol/L – which investigation helps decide if the loss is renal or gastrointestinal? — Spot urine K⁺/creatinine ratio; a high ratio indicates renal loss.
Why must magnesium be corrected before giving potassium in refractory hypokalaemia? — Magnesium is required for Na⁺/K⁺‑ATPase activity; without it, potassium cannot be retained intracellularly.

A malaria‑positive adult with severe diarrhoea has K⁺ 2.4 mmol/L and ECG showing U‑waves – what red‑flag complication should you monitor for? — Ventricular arrhythmias; continuous ECG monitoring is essential.
How does re‑feeding syndrome cause hypokalaemia and what preventive step is taken? — Insulin surge drives K⁺ into cells; start low‑dose potassium supplementation before nutrition is advanced.
What distinguishes hypokalaemia from hyperkalaemia on ECG? — Hypokalaemia shows flattened T‑waves and U‑waves; hyperkalaemia shows peaked T‑waves and widened QRS.
A patient on spironolactone develops hyperkalaemia; why would you avoid this drug in a hypokalaemic patient? — It is a potassium‑sparing diuretic and would worsen low serum potassium.
In a resource‑limited setting without serum electrolytes, what clinical clues suggest hypokalaemia? — Muscle weakness, constipation, arrhythmic pulse, and history of diarrhoea or diuretic use.
